slides.title: Introduction to Phishing
slides.description:
Definition of phishing

The fraudulent practice of sending emails or other messages purporting to be from reputable companies in order to induce individuals to reveal personal information, such as passwords and credit card numbers.

Importance of recognizing phishing attacks

This awareness helps make you more resilient to cyber-attacks, creating a robust defense against threats. It's a great way to help your team spot phishing attacks, keeping everyone's data safer. Acts as a refresher on the company's cyber security policies and procedures.

Examples of real-world consequences of successful phishing attacks

  • Data Loss
  • Damaged Reputation
  • Direct Monetary Loss
  • Loss of Productivity
  • Loss of Customers
  • Financial Penalties
  • Intellectual Property
  • Loss of Companies Value

slides.title: Types of Phishing Attacks
slides.description:
Email phishing- Phishing is a type of online scam that targets consumers by sending them an email that appears to be from a well-known source - an internet service provider, a bank, or a mortgage company, for example.

Spear phishing- The fraudulent practice of sending emails ostensibly from a known or trusted sender in order to induce targeted individuals to reveal confidential information.

Whaling- Whaling is a highly targeted phishing attack - aimed at a senior executives - masquerading as a legitimate email. Whaling is digitally enabled fraud through social engineering, designed to encourage victims to perform a secondary action, such as initiating a wire transfer of funds.

Vishing- Vishing, short for voice phishing, uses fraudulent phone calls to trick victims into providing sensitive information, like login credentials, credit card numbers, or bank details.

Smishing (SMS phishing)- Smishing is a form of phishing that specifically targets users through text messages.

Social media phishing- Is used by attackers seeking to steal personal data to sell on dark web or to gain access, typically to financial accounts.

Clone phishing H. Pharming- Pharming (a play on the words “phishing” and “farming”) occurs when an attacker alters your computer or router's settings to redirect legitimate users to malicious sites.

slides.title: Techniques Used in Phishing Attacks
slides.description:
Social engineering tactics- 5 most common are:

  1. Baiting
  2. Scareware
  3. Pretexting
  4. Phishing
  5. Spear Phishing

Spoofing- Utilizing cybersecurity that involves scammers pretending to be someone else to steal data or money or to spread malware.

Malicious attachments- email attachments are an increasingly dangerous threat to corporate security. Disguised as documents, voicemails, e-faxes or PDFs, malicious email attachments are an attack on the victim’s computer when the attachment is opened.

Malicious links- Are disguised as documents, voicemails, e-faxes or PDFs, malicious email attachments are designed to launch an attack on the victim's computer when the attachment is opened.

Domain spoofing- Domain spoofing is when cyber criminals fake a website name or email domain to try to fool users.

Impersonation- Example “Online Identity Theft”: Impersonating someone on social media or creating fake profiles to deceive others.

slides.title: Identifying Phishing Emails
slides.description:
• Suspicious sender email addresses
  • Grammatical and spelling errors
  • Requests for sensitive information
  • Urgency or threats
  • Unexpected attachments or links
  • Spoofed URLs
  • Unusual sender behavior

slides.title: Best Practices for Avoiding Phishing Attacks
slides.description:
• Think before clicking
  • Verify the sender’s identity
  • Check URLs before clicking
  • Be cautious with attachments and downloads
  • Use multi-factor authentication
  • Keep software updated
  • Report suspicious emails

questions.question: In the script, a phishing campaign is best described as:

answers.a: A one-time password reset request from IT
answers.b: A large-scale, coordinated effort to trick people into revealing sensitive info or taking harmful actions
answers.c: A software update that improves security

answers.a: A phishing attempt sent through a text/SMS message
answers.b: A phone call pretending to be customer support
answers.c: A fake website that copies a real login page
answers.d: A malware program that encrypts files

questions.question: Phishing campaigns mainly rely on technical hacking tools, not human behavior.
Which of the following is Personally Identifiable Information (P.I.I.) mentioned in the script?

answers.a: Copying legitimate emails and swapping links/attachments to trick recipients
answers.b: Copying a computer hard drive for backups

answers.c: High-level executives like CEOs and CFOs
